newsitem.title: UK: PNG coffee crop seen up, no impact from army revol.
newsitem.headline: PNG coffee crop seen up, no impact from army revol.

text.p: Papua New Guinea is expected to produce 1.1-1.2 million 60-kg bags of coffee in calendar 1997, up from just over 1.0 million in 1996, an industry official said on Tuesday.

Mick Wheeler, the London representative for the PNG Coffee Industry Corp, also told Reuters that the current political confrontation between the military and government in PNG was unlikely to hurt coffee shipments. PNG produces a mere one percent of world coffee.
PNG Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said on Tuesday his government was in "absolute control" of the South Pacific nation after the sacking of army chief Jerry Singirok.

Singirok brought about one of the worst crises in PNG's 22 years of independence when he gave Chan an ultimatum to quit over his decision to use mercenaries against a rebellion on Bougainville island.
The copper-rich Bougainville is situated about 400 km from the mainland, where most of the coffee is grown.

Wheeler also said the expected slight increase in the 1997 crop followed the recent rally in world prices which lifted New York arabica futures by more than 50 percent since early January before falling back from this week.
Almost all of PNG's coffee is the arabica type of beans. Production of robusta amounts to just 50,000 bags a year.

Traders said coffee arrivals from PNG were gaining momentum but added that the first major shipments of the main May-July crop were not expected until the end of April if the favourable weather prevailed.
They noted encouraging roaster demand for the main crop but sellers were hesitant, holding back on hopes of much higher prices.
About 85 percent of PNG's coffee is destined for Germany and Australia, its two traditional markets. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
